2026_362_6_e_25_26_budget_amendment_3_re.paragraph: Consent item 6.E. at the Troy School District Board of Education's regular meeting of June 16, 2026 presented the third budget amendment resolution for the 2025-26 fiscal year, covering the General Fund, Sinking Fund, Food Service Fund, Troy Career Center Fund, Community Service Fund, Preschool Fund and Debt Service Fund. The resolution amends General Fund appropriations to $207,641,522 against total available to appropriate of $235,866,839, leaving a projected June 30, 2026 ending fund balance of $28,225,317. Administration recommended adoption and noted the resolution need not be read in full but must be entered into the official minutes.

**Item**

Blank lines are provided for Moved By, Supported By, and Yes/No vote tallies.

**General Fund**
Revenues move from an amended budget of $197,760,255 to a proposed amended budget of $202,153,044, a change of $4,392,789. Fund balance July 1, 2025 is unchanged at $33,713,795, giving total available to appropriate of $235,866,839 versus $231,474,050. Total expenditures and outgoing transfers rise from $203,763,818 to $207,641,522, a change of $3,877,704. Excess revenues (expenditures) moves from $(6,003,563) to $(5,488,478), a change of $515,085, and the June 30, 2026 ending fund balance from $27,710,232 to $28,225,317.

The Debt Service Funds amendment is the largest, with local revenue amended from $32,218,308 to $57,194,507 and debt service expenditure from $32,070,536 to $57,686,180. 2026_363_6_f_26_27_budget_adoption_resol.paragraph: Consent item 6.F. at the Troy School District Board of Education's June 16, 2026 regular meeting is the 2026-27 Budget Appropriation Resolution, adopting general appropriations and millage rates for ten funds including the General Fund, Food Service Fund, Troy Career Center Fund, Community Service Fund, Preschool Fund, Troy School and Student Activities Fund, Debt Service Funds, Capital Maintenance Fund, 2023 Capital Projects Fund and Sinking Fund. The General Fund is appropriated at $193,342,088 against total revenues of $191,055,509 and an estimated July 1 fund balance of $28,225,317. Millage levies set are 18.0000 mills non-homestead operating, 8.4102 mills commercial personal property, 2.4102 mills homestead, 6.1000 mills debt retirement and 0.9473 mills sinking fund.

Consent agenda item 6.F. at the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting of June 16, 2026 is the 2026-27 Budget Appropriation Resolution. The cover memorandum states the attached Appropriations Resolution for fiscal year 2026-27 includes the General Fund, Food Service Fund, Troy Career Center Fund, Community Service Fund, Troy School District Preschool Fund, Troy School and Student Activities Fund, Debt Fund, Capital Maintenance Fund, 2023 Capital Projects Fund and Sinking Fund, that approval is recommended, and that the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes. Moved By, Supported By and Yes/No lines are left blank. The operative clause resolves that the general appropriations and budget and millage rates of the Troy School District for fiscal year 2026-27 be approved and made part of the official minutes of the June 16, 2026 regular meeting.

MILLAGE RATES. The tax base schedule lists Non-Homestead, General Operating, 18.0000 mills; Commercial Personal Property, General Operating, 8.4102 mills; Homestead, General Operating, 2.4102 mills; All Properties, Debt Retirement, 6.1000 mills; All Properties, Sinking Fund, 0.9473 mills. The narrative resolving clause repeats that for operating purposes 18.0000 mills be levied on non-homesteads and 2.4102 mills on homesteads and industrial personal property, that 8.4102 mills be levied on commercial personal property, that 6.10 mills be levied on all classes of property for debt retirement, and that 0.9473 mills be levied on all classes of property for sinking fund purposes.

2026_364_6i_2026_spring_proposed_new_res.paragraph: Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) circulated a proposed new resolution for member district consideration in May 2026, stating that OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege. The rationale cites the FY26 school aid budget's section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding, which required districts to opt in and, in doing so, to agree to cooperate with an investigation including waiving attorney-client privilege following a mass-casualty incident. The packet also reprints OCSBA's continuing resolutions for reference, noting under OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5 that resolutions approved by at least nineteen member school districts become the official position of the association.
2026_364_6i_2026_spring_proposed_new_res.page:
**Proposed new resolution (May 2026)**
OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege.

**Rationale**
In the FY26 school aid budget, section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to "opt in." Any district that opted in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation, including waiving the attorney-client privilege, following a mass-casualty incident. The rationale argues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass casualty event is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, that the courts have ruled on this issue, and that nothing would stop the legislature from tying waiver of the privilege to other funding in the future.

**Adoption threshold**
OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. The continuing resolutions that follow are provided for reference only, with adoption and amendment dates noted.

**Continuing resolutions**

| Resolution | Adopted / amended |
| --- | --- |
| Accountability and Transparency | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Broadband Access and Devices | 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Early Childhood | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Early On Michigan | 1/26/2026 |
| Evidence-Based Decision Making | 9/24/2019 |
| Lame Duck | 9/24/2019 |
| Local Control | 9/24/2019 |
| Mental Health | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Non-Partisan Elections | 1/9/2026 |
| School Aid | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| School Finance Research Collaborative | 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023, 6/5/2025 |
| School Nutrition | 3/3/2023; amended 6/5/2025 |
| School Safety | 3/3/2023 |
| Special Education | 9/24/2019 |
| Teacher Shortages | 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Unfunded Mandates | 9/24/2019 |

**Selected positions**
Accountability and Transparency applies the same standards, including FOIA and the Open Meetings Act, to local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities. Early Childhood supports new dollars for universal public preschool for all four-year-olds and mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-olds. School Aid asks that the School Aid Fund be constitutionally restricted to Pre-K through 12th grade public education, opposes private school vouchers or tax credit programs, supports added funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students, protects the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes, and urges enactment of the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts can meet the June 30 budget deadline. Special Education supports full funding of IDEA, noting federal legislation initially promised 40 percent of the excess cost. The School Finance Research Collaborative resolution supports implementing SFRC recommendations while holding higher funded districts harmless.

**Aligned agendas**
When aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the NSBA, MASB, Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) and COSSBA legislative agendas.
2026_364_6i_2026_spring_proposed_new_res.verbose:
This three-page Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) packet, labeled "Proposed NEW Resolution May, 2026" and carried as item 6I on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for the meeting dated June 16, 2026, presents one proposed new resolution for member district consideration together with the association's full slate of continuing resolutions.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTION: "OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege." The stated rationale is that in the FY26 school aid budget, section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to "opt in," and any district that opted in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation, including waiving the attorney-client privilege, following a mass-casualty incident. The rationale continues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass casualty event is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, that the courts have ruled on this issue, and that in the future there is nothing to stop the legislature from tying waiver of the attorney-client privilege to other funding.

ADOPTION MECHANISM. The continuing resolutions are stated to have been adopted by member school districts and are provided for reference only, with adoption and/or amendment dates noted for each. OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption, provides that resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: OCSBA supports holding every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (aka Charter Schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities. Cited as MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f).

BROADBAND ACCESS AND DEVICES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021; Amended 6/5/2025]: broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding opportunities to expand affordable and reliable broadband access; supports federal and state programs for purchase of internet capable devices and software; and supports dedicated resources for cybersecurity. Cited as MASB Resolution A-10.30 (2021 amendment).

EARLY CHILDHOOD [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports additional new dollars to fund universal, public preschool for all four-year-old children, and mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-old children. Cited as MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c).

EARLY ON MICHIGAN [OCSBA Adopted 1/26/2026]: supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions.

EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student. Cited as MASB Resolution G 11.01.

LAME DUCK [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports lame duck parameters addressing introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.

LOCAL CONTROL [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards. Cited as MASB Resolutions A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70.

MENTAL HEALTH [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and providing, at a minimum, annual inflation adjusted state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe; help staff identify potential mental health issues for students; encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response. Cited as MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50.

NON-PARTISAN ELECTIONS [OCSBA Adopted 1/9/2026]: supports non-partisan school board elections.

SCHOOL AID [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025], four parts: (A) specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school vouchers or tax credit programs [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05]; (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j); A 10.55]; (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c); A 10.55]; (D) support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional/statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30 [MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h)].

SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021; 3/3/2023; 6/5/2025]: supports implementation of the recommendations of the SFRC, while requiring that higher funded districts be held harmless. Cited as MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 (2021 amendment).

SCHOOL NUTRITION [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports codification of free universal meals.

SCHOOL SAFETY [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023]: supports adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

SPECIAL EDUCATION [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local school districts to make up the difference. Cited as MASB Resolution A 5.01 and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA.

TEACHER SHORTAGES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, potentially including incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states. Cited as MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

UNFUNDED MANDATES [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose any federal laws or programs that are not fully funded and thus cost the state valuable resources. Cited as MASB Resolution A 10.20.

WHEN ALIGNED WITH OCSBA LEGISLATIVE PRIORITIES, OCSBA ALSO SUPPORTS [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda; the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda; the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda; and the Consortium of State School Board Associations (COSSBA) Legislative Agenda.

LINKS provided: MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy; COSSBA Advocacy at https://www.cossba.org/advocacy.

2026_366_mhsaa_cooperative_agreement_req.paragraph: Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) high school cooperative agreement packet attached to the Troy School District Board of Education agenda of July 22, 2026 in support of a Troy Athens boys lacrosse cooperative team request for 2026-27. The packet reproduces MHSAA Handbook Regulation I, Section 1(E) and 1(F) and their interpretations, the procedures for application, renewal and dissolution, advance preparation materials, and the blank two-page Senior High Application to Form and Support a Cooperative Team. Under Section 1(F)(1), boys lacrosse is among the sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools for which two or more member high schools with combined enrollment not exceeding 3,500 students may operate a cooperative program with Executive Committee approval.
2026_366_mhsaa_cooperative_agreement_req.page:
**What this is**
MHSAA "High School Cooperative Agreement Regulations, Procedures and Advance Preparation Material to Assist Schools," together with the blank two-page Senior High Application to Form and Support a Cooperative Team, submitted with a Troy Athens boys lacrosse cooperative request for 2026-27. Completed forms are emailed to coops@mhsaa.com.

**Enrollment thresholds (Regulation I, Section 1)**

| Provision | Enrollment ceiling | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sect. 1(E) | 1,000 combined | Any sport |
| Sect. 1(E-1) | none | Subvarsity only, any sport |
| Sect. 1(E-2) | none | Named sports, same public school district |
| Sect. 1(F-1) | 3,500 combined | Sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools |
| Sect. 1(F-2) | 5,500 combined | Ice hockey |
| Sect. 1(F-3)/(F-4) | waiver, four years | New or previously dropped sponsorship |

The Section 1(F)(1) sport list is field hockey, gymnastics, boys lacrosse, girls lacrosse, boys alpine skiing, girls alpine skiing, boys swimming & diving, girls swimming & diving, boys tennis, girls tennis and boys volleyball. Section 1(E-2) names baseball, bowling, competitive cheer, cross country, field hockey, golf, boys and girls lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis, boys volleyball and wrestling for two or more schools of the same public school district.

**Deadlines**
New cooperative programs: May 1 for fall sports, Aug. 15 for winter sports, Oct. 15 for spring sports. Dissolution deadlines are the same three dates. Renewal forms for agreements including a Class A or B school, or three or more schools, are due every two years prior to May 1, emailed to the primary school in March/April. A league may void an agreement at renewal by notification prior to April 1 of the previous school year. Section 1(F-3)/(F-4) four-year programs must report plans to the MHSAA by February 1 of the final year.

**Application requirements**
Application must be made on MHSAA forms by the administration of the cooperating member schools and be accompanied by (1) a resolution of authorization by each board of education describing the purpose for sponsoring the program and the Advance Preparation Materials, indicating which school or district administers it locally, and (2) a resolution of support from each league or conference, or support from at least four future opponents if there is no league. One school must be designated primary host and becomes the official team name. Enrollment figures come from the most recent Enrollment Declaration Form. Agreements are effective for two years.

**Executive Committee criteria**
Lack of numbers of students to support a program; lack of qualified staff to coach; lack of facilities; and evidence of a desire to increase opportunities for participation in new programs rather than win/loss records of existing programs.

**Advance preparation and guidelines**
Schools are asked to settle in writing who pays for and maintains uniforms, equipment and facilities; travel to practices and contests; selection, supervision and payment of coaches; cheerleaders; training rules and letter award guidelines; academic regulations; class schedule coordination; gate receipts; practice and game sites; hosting and supervision; athletic accident insurance and liability notification; and school identity, mascot and colors. A Cooperative Program Board of Control including at least an administrator and the athletic director of each school should oversee the program. The MHSAA Representative Council reaffirms its preference that Class A and B schools sponsor separate teams rather than repeatedly renew cooperative programs.

**Signatures required**
Superintendent, Board of Education, Principal and Athletic Director signatures plus date for each cooperating school.
2026_366_mhsaa_cooperative_agreement_req.verbose:
The document attached to the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for July 22, 2026 under the title "MHSAA Cooperative Agreement Request - Troy Athens - Boys Lacrosse - 26-27" is the Michigan High School Athletic Association's standard packet, "High School Cooperative Agreement Regulations, Procedures and Advance Preparation Material to Assist Schools," followed by the blank two-page Senior High Application to Form and Support a Cooperative Team with its Board of Education resolution page.

MHSAA HANDBOOK REGULATION I, SECTION 1(E). In any sport, two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 1,000 students may conduct, with Executive Committee approval, a Cooperative Program in the specific sports applied for. Subsection 1 allows the Executive Committee to approve a cooperative program at the subvarsity level only, in any sport, for two or more member high schools regardless of enrollment; there must be a demonstrated history of inadequate numbers of participants and approval will not be granted based on financial concerns. Students in such programs hold varsity eligibility only with their school of actual enrollment if brought up to a varsity team during the regular season or MHSAA Tournament. A student who participates in a subvarsity cooperative program and transfers into another school in that program may not be the subject of a waiver request under Regulation I, Section 9(C). Deadlines for high school cooperative programs and the two-year minimum operating length do not apply, but board of education, league (or four future opponents) and Executive Committee approvals are required. Subsection 2 allows approval regardless of combined enrollment maximum in baseball, bowling, competitive cheer, cross country, field hockey, golf, boys and girls lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis, boys volleyball and wrestling for two or more schools of the same public school district under the same governing board; a demonstrated history of low participation is required, financial concerns are not a basis, the allowance does not apply to public school academies, approval is case-by-case, league or conference approval is required, and the standard deadlines apply.

SECTION 1(F). (1) Two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 3,500 students may conduct, with Executive Committee approval, a Cooperative Program in specific sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools: field hockey, gymnastics, boys lacrosse, girls lacrosse, boys alpine skiing, girls alpine skiing, boys swimming & diving, girls swimming & diving, boys tennis, girls tennis and boys volleyball. (2) Two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 5,500 students may conduct a Cooperative Program in ice hockey. (3) For those 12 sports, if none of the schools involved sponsored the sport at any level on an interscholastic basis during the previous school year, the 3,500 or 5,500 (ice hockey only) maximum may be waived by the Executive Committee, but the cooperative agreement may not exist beyond four school years. (4) The Executive Committee may approve an agreement in excess of the 3,500 or 5,500 maximum for up to four years in sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools if during the previous year the school, or the cooperative program the school was part of, dropped the sport because of demonstrated lack of participation; again limited to four school years.

INTERPRETATIONS (items 12-14). Cooperative Programs are arrangements made for a minimum of two years but may be voided at any time by resolutions of any cooperating board of education; if voided before completion of the second year, the terminating school or schools may not enter another cooperative program in the sports involved until another two-year period has transpired. Deadlines for dissolution are May 1 for fall sports, Aug. 15 for winter sports and Oct. 15 for spring sports; dissolutions after those dates may not permit changes to tournament divisions or assignments. Agreements established under Section 1(E) whose combined enrollments later rise above 1,000 students as established each February will be dissolved prior to the start of the school year in which the new enrollment is effective. If combined enrollment exceeds the original Division in the second year of an agreement, the schools play in the higher Division of MHSAA tournaments in the cooperative sports. A new MHSAA member school otherwise ineligible for tournaments until its second full year may participate sooner if it joins a Cooperative Program with a tournament-eligible member school. If the MHSAA Membership Resolution for a school in a cooperative agreement is not submitted on or before the fourth Friday after Labor Day, students of that school may not participate in any MHSAA tournament, including cooperative sports. Agreements including a Class A or B school, or three or more schools, must submit a renewal form every two years prior to May 1; the form is emailed to the primary school in March and requires league approval and statistics on participation levels and win/loss records. Agreements involving only two Class C or D schools need not submit renewal forms and continue until the MHSAA is notified of dissolution or a league withdraws support. After the initial two years, a league may by vote of its membership void an agreement at renewal by notifying all schools and the MHSAA prior to April 1 of the previous school year. Adding new schools requires a new application with all approvals. Programs started in newly sponsored sports under Section 1(F) over the 3,500 limit complete the two-year renewal process and are automatically dissolved after the fourth year. Cooperative Programs in sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools are assigned tournament classification corresponding to total enrollment of the cooperating schools. When a sport is removed from the Section 1(F) list, existing programs are grandfathered subject to Executive Committee review at each renewal. Section 1(F) four-year programs must report to the MHSAA by February 1 of the final school year how the schools and teams will operate under 3,500/5,500 students subsequently. Programs whose combined enrollment on the February Enrollment Declaration Form exceeds 3,500/5,500 or the Section 1(E) limit may not operate in the coming school year. Deadlines for newly forming programs are May 1 (fall), Aug. 15 (winter) and Oct. 15 (spring); where a school is established and opened after the fall and winter deadlines, application may be made until MHSAA tournament assignments are made or Oct. 15, whichever occurs first.

PROCEDURES. Applications must be made on MHSAA forms by the administration of the cooperating member schools and received, even if partially completed, by the stated deadline; subvarsity-only and middle school applications have no established deadline but need board, league and Executive Committee approval before operating. Each application must include a resolution of authorization by each board of education describing the purpose for sponsoring the program and the Advance Preparation Materials and indicating which school or district will oversee local administration, plus a resolution of support from each league or conference, or from at least four future opponents if the schools do not belong to a league. One school must be designated primary host on the application and is considered the official team name; all signatures and enrollment figures from the most recent Enrollment Declaration Form must be provided. The Executive Committee considers lack of numbers of students to support a program, lack of qualified staff to coach, lack of facilities, and evidence of a desire to increase opportunities for participation in new programs rather than win/loss records of existing programs. Agreements are effective for two years, and no other cooperative agreement in the same sports may be made with another school until the original two-year period lapses; agreements may be voided in writing or via the Cooperative Program Dissolution Form. Renewal rules mirror the interpretations above, with the renewal form emailed to the primary school each April. A note records that the MHSAA Representative Council reaffirms its preference that Class A and B schools sponsor separate teams rather than continue to renew cooperative programs over a period of years without careful evaluation, and that schools should review participation numbers annually.

ADVANCE PREPARATION MATERIALS. Schools are asked to consider whether students from another school will replace students from their own community in an existing program, and, where two or more schools are creating a program where none existed, who pays for and maintains or launders uniforms, equipment and facilities; who pays travel to practices and contests; who selects, supervises and pays coaches; whose cheerleaders will cheer; whose training rules and letter award guidelines apply; whose local academic and other regulations apply; whether daily class schedules can be coordinated; how gate receipts are handled; where practices and games are held and who pays those expenses; who hosts and supervises events; whether athletic accident insurance is provided, who pays for it and whether liability insurers have been notified; and whose school identity, mascot and colors will be used. Schools must also consider whether an existing sport will suffer from creation of a cooperative program in another sport that season.

GUIDELINES. All issues should be addressed in writing in advance and submitted with the application for future reference. A "Cooperative Program Board of Control" consisting of at least an administrator and the athletic director of each cooperating school should be appointed to initiate the program and resolve disputes. Cooperating districts should be adjacent, though not required, with reasonable travel distance. Cooperative arrangements should be sought only where opportunities are limited and students are not expected to be cut. Agreements are intended for a significant group of students over several years, not a single participant for a year or two. There is no limit on the number of schools in an agreement, but programs with several schools tend to resemble non-school sports and may blur the philosophy of school sports.

APPLICATION FORM. The blank Senior High application collects the sport(s) with boys/girls designation, the primary and up to five secondary high schools with city, enrollment and class, the Handbook regulation under which the agreement is formed (Sect. 1[E], 1[E-1], 1[E-2], 1[F-1], 1[F-2], 1[F-3], 1[F-4]), the team levels sponsored (V, JV, Freshman), whether any school sponsored the sport last year, whether the schools have a current agreement in another sport, an acknowledgment that the agreement commences and continues for a minimum of two years, attached written support from the applicable league or four future opponents, certification that all approvals, required study, planning and review are complete, and whether the team will be known by a name other than a school name (the MHSAA generally uses the primary school as the designated team title). Page 2 is the Cooperative Program Board of Control resolution, submitted with the application and letter of league support, requiring Superintendent, Board of Education, Principal and Athletic Director signatures and dates for each cooperating school, plus the name, school represented, phone and email of the person completing the application. Completed forms are emailed to coops@mhsaa.com.
